items.title: ‘The Altruists’ review: another cautionary tale of power, corruption and tech bros
items.summary:
F or better or worse, tech bros make compelling television. The arrogance! The talent! Those closeted sociopathic tendencies! The latest show to explore how those qualities might be a bad thing, actually, is The Altruists . Like The Social Reckoning , it’s about a few maths geeks who thought they could hit the big time by moving fast and breaking things. And like You Can See Everything , it’s about what happens when that dream collides headfirst with reality, and takes a few billion pounds in customer money along with it.

READ MORE: ‘You Can See Everything’ review: a three-hour odyssey of deception, doubt and dodgy dealings 

This eight-part Netflix series follows real-life antiheroes Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison who were convicted in 2024 of various counts of money laundering, wire-tapping and fraud linked to their cryptocurrency exchange, FTX.

Here, the pair are played by Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, in performances better than the script (or their wigs) really allow for. When we first meet them, it’s on the verge of disaster. It’s 2022 and FTX is riding high enough to fund a lavish party in the Bahamas, with speakers including Tony Blair and Bill Clinton. But behind the scenes, things are falling apart.

Bank sheet discrepancies are coming to light and whispers of fraud are in the air. Tensions are high. How did this happen? The series sets about finding out, by rapidly shuffling us back and forwards in time to examine just how their dream went so badly wrong.

First they sacrifice their ethics, then they start throwing other people under the bus. Though…
items.t: ‘The Altruists’ review: another cautionary tale of power, corruption and tech bros

items.title: CISAC’s International Standard Musical Work Codes System Hits 100 Million Songs Milestone
items.summary:
CISAC (the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers) says its International Standard Musical Work Codes system — the tracking mechanism it created to identify and track individual songs — has hit the 100 million songs milestone.

“Behind every code is a song, a story, and the people who created it, CISAC’s director of business and technology said in a statement. “CISAC’s priority is to strengthen the connection between accurate data and fair remuneration for the creators the system serves.”

Related 

CISAC Reports Record Global Creator Royalties, Warns of ‘Largest Test’ From AI 

Rod Wave Indicted on Drug & Gun Charges for Items Allegedly Found in Car After Speeding Stop 

CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment 

The first work assigned an ISWC code, or T-000.000.001.0, was ABBA’s “Dancing Queen” 30 years ago.

The code is an essential ingredient in ensuring songwriters get paid, especially in today’s world, where multiple collection societies around the globe track activity for each song, many of which have multiple songwriters. Each code provides a unique, permanent reference for a musical work, connecting it to information about its authors and composers, the announcement says, adding it has become key in sharing musical works data across the global network of song collection management organizations, also known as performance rights organizations in the U.S. Today, more than 100 societies around the globe are using the new system.

CISAC adds that close to 30 publishers are allocating ISWCs…
items.t: CISAC’s International Standard Musical Work Codes System Hits 100 Million Songs Milestone

items.title: 50 Cent Steps Out With Reebok G-Unit G6 Reboot
items.summary:
Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson ‘s reboot with Reebok is making a comeback, just in time for Christmas.

The hip-hop veteran recently teamed up with the sportswear specialist for the G-Unit G6, a blast from the past sneaker which were unveiled in August in its original red, white and blue colorway and proved to be a hit with 50 Cent’s followers. Those shoes re-launch globally on Friday, Nov. 20 .

The basketball and street fashion-inspired gear initially rolled out in 2003, the year when Fifty blew up on airwaves and charts around the globe. The one that got away, “In Da Club,” logged nine weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100, and the New Yorker followed it up two months later with “21 Questions,” featuring the late Nate Dogg, which spent a full month atop the national singles survey. His smash album Get Rich or Die Tryin’ held the top spot on the Billboard 200 for six weeks, and lent its name to the 2005 semi-autobiographical film, which gave 50 Cent his first starring role.

That partnership made Jackson one of the first musicians to lead a major footwear franchise. “Creating it the first time was special,” Jackson recounts in an interview with GQ . “I worked with Todd (Krinsky) and the team on everything and they really let me make it mine. It wasn’t just a sneaker—it became part of the culture.”

Krinsky, who started with Reebok in 1993, working in the mailroom, is now CEO. “Our relationship with 50 has always gone beyond sneakers,” he remarks in a statement. “He helped define an important chapter in Reebok’s history, and together we created something that had a lasting impact on…
items.t: 50 Cent Steps Out With Reebok G-Unit G6 Reboot

items.title: ‘Never Go Backwards, Just Make Things Bigger and Better’: How Paul O’Neill Chartered Trans-Siberian Orchestra’s Journey Ahead
items.summary:
When Trans-Siberian Orchestra turned 20 back in 2016, the troupe’s enduring success was as surprising to founder Paul O’Neill as anyone in or outside of the camp.

“I would love to say that we planned for it to resonate like this, but it was just pure luck,” acknowledged O’Neill, who passed away the following year at the age of 61 . And that it was an endeavor almost entirely based around the Christmas holiday made it seem even less likely.

“Normally you have five or six other platinum albums, then you take on Christmas,” O’Neill noted. “Of course, we took it on first and the rest of the year on later. It’s all worked out.”

That’s certainly an understatement for TSO, which celebrates the 30th anniversary of its triple-platinum debut album, Christmas Eve and Other Stories , this year with its annual, two-company concert tour opening Nov. 19 in Green Bay, Wisc., and Council Bluffs, Iowa. The 97 performances through Dec. 30 will again feature the soundtrack and narration from The Ghosts of Christmas Eve , TSO’s 1999 made-for-TV film, and other material amidst the usual fusillade of arena-filling special effects and pyrotechnics, with two shows a day at most stops.

During the past three decades TSO has released six studio albums — four platinum or better, three Christmas-themed — and an EP, along with the multi-platinum singles “Christmas Eve/Sarajevo 12/24” and “Christmas Cannon.” The 2005 track “Wizards in Winter” also hit platinum, and a fan’s synchronized home display soundtracked by the tune was turned into an ad campaign for Miller Lite.

items.title: John Christ, Guitarist With Danzig, Dies at 61
items.summary:
John Christ , the veteran electric guitarist who wielded the axe for Danzig and Samhain and was widely recognized by the metal community as one of the best to do it, has passed away following a battle with poor health. He was 61.

“It is with a heavy heart that we must inform you of the peaceful passing of John Christ on November 15, 2026,” reads a statement posted on Danzig’s socials.

“No services are planned and we kindly ask everyone to respect the family’s privacy during this time,” the post continues. “John loved each and every one of you.”

View this post on Instagram 

Born John Wolfgang Knoll, in Baltimore, Maryland, the youngest and only boy of five kids, the future rocker got a relatively traditional music education, initially on the piano before picking up the acoustic guitar, and then plugged in at age 13. Both his parents were accomplished musicians.

In the late ‘80s he dropped out of college, relocated to New Jersey and joined forces with ex- Misfits frontman Glenn Danzig on the black-as-night rock band Samhain , which would later become Danzig. Christ auditioned for the spot, and caught the attention of Danzig and Rick Rubin, who was scouting acts for his record label, Def Jam Recordings, with a performance that was both brutal and bloody, thanks to strumming finger gashed on the strings.

The anecdote is retold on Christ’s biography . “Accidentally brushing up against Glenn, he left five bloody lines on his shoulder. Rubin thought this was awesome—Danzig did not agree—he thought Christ was on speed,” it reads. When he didn’t receive an immediate callback,…

items.title: The Biggest Snubs & Surprises at the 2026 CMA Awards
items.summary:
Everyone expected Ella Langley to sweep the 2026 CMA Awards , and sure enough, she did, setting a new, all-time record of six awards in one night. That broke the old record of five awards in one night first set by Johnny Cash in 1969 and then tied by Vince Gill in 1993, Alan Jackson in 2002 and Lainey Wilson in 2023.

But that doesn’t mean there were no snubs or surprises at the awards show, which was held at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville on Wednesday (Nov. 18) and hosted by Wilson for the third year in a row (second year in a row as solo host).

Related 

Here Are the 2026 CMA Awards Winners: Full List 

The show opened with a tribute to Dolly Parton, who died in August, with Vince Gill and Wilson singing the country icon’s 1974 classic “I Will Always Love You.” There was also a tribute to John Anderson, who died in October, with Dierks Bentley and Zach Top singing his 1983 hit “Swingin.’”

Perhaps because it was the show’s 60th anniversary, there were several backward-looking performances. Taylor Swift included a bit of her 2007 hit “Our Song” (her first No. 1 hit on Billboard ’s Hot Country Songs chart) in her performance of her current hit “I Knew It, I Knew You.” Tim McGraw performed his 1994 hit “Don’t Take the Girl” ( his first No. 1 on Hot Country Songs). Tucker Wetmore performed Hank Williams Jr.’s 1984 hit “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight.” Brooks & Dunn performed a hit medley.

But let’s get back to what you came for: Here are snubs and surprises from the 2026 CMA Awards.
items.t: The Biggest Snubs & Surprises at the 2026 CMA Awards

items.title: Ella Langley & More Record-Setters at the 2026 CMA Awards
items.summary:
Ella Langley set a new, all-time record for most CMA Awards wins in one night on Wednesday (Nov. 18). Langley won six awards, breaking the old record of five wins in one night first set by Johnny Cash in 1969 and then tied by Vince Gill in 1993, Alan Jackson in 2002 and Lainey Wilson in 2023.

Langley has won 10 CMA Awards in just three years. Only two other female solo artists and one all-female group have won 10 or more CMA Awards. Miranda Lambert upped her total of wins to 17 this year. Wilson has won 12 (though she didn’t add to her tally this year). The Chicks have won 10.

Langley, 27, became the second-youngest entertainer of the year winner in CMA history. Taylor Swift was even younger, 19, when she won in that category for the first time in 2009. (She was 21 when she won for a second time two years later.)

Related 

Here Are the 2026 CMA Awards Winners: Full List 

Langley won entertainer one year after Wilson won in the category for a second time. This is the second time in CMA history that female acts (solo artists or all-female groups) have won back-to-back awards in this category. The first was when Shania Twain won in 1999, followed by The Chicks in 2000.

Langley won single, song and video of the year for her smash “Choosin’ Texas.” She won in all three categories last year in tandem with Riley Green for their sexy duet “You Look Like You Love Me.” She’s the first artist to achieve this three-award sweep twice. The Brooks & Dunn classic “Believe” won all three awards in 2006.

items.title: Sex Pistols’ Glen Matlock reveals work on first Faces album since 1973: “Never a dull moment”
items.summary:
Sex Pistols ’ Glen Matlock has revealed that he has worked with Faces for what will be their first album since 1973.

READ MORE: Ronnie Wood talks new Jimi Hendrix exhibition and hopes of Rolling Stones tour: “When my compadres say, ‘Let’s go’, I’ll be ready” 

The band, which features Rod Stewart , Ronnie Wood and drummer Kenney Jones, formed in 1969 from the ashes of Small Faces . In their time together, Faces recorded four studio albums, the last of which being ‘Ooh La La’, which dropped back in 1973.

They formally disbanded in 1975 after Stewart left the group, and around that time, Wood began playing with The Rolling Stones . Founding bassist Ronnie Lane passed away in 1997, and keyboardist Ian McLagan died of a stroke back in 2014 .

There has been speculation for years now that a reunion could be back on the table, and rumours gained momentum in 2020, when the three surviving members came together to perform a live rendition of ‘Stay With Me’ at that year’s BRIT Awards .

The following year, Wood spoke to The Times and said that he and his bandmates had “been recording some new Faces music”, and Stewart also teased that the trio had completed “15 tracks that are extremely worthy, some old, some new”. Jones went on to make a similar statement , saying that they had “a mixture of stuff we never released which is worthy of releasing” as well as “some new stuff which is really wonderful”.

Now, it looks like fans are one step closer to getting a new Faces album, as Sex Pistols’ bassist Glen Matlock shared a post online, seemingly…

items.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ fans are pretending they’re in New Zealand to play the game early
items.summary:
Some Grand Theft Auto 6 fans have tricked their console into thinking they’re in New Zealand so they can play the game early.

READ MORE: ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ review: one of the best games ever made 

Rather than a global release, Grand Theft Auto 6 officially launches midnight November 19 local time . It means that gamers in New Zealand can return to Vice City a full 19 hours before those living in America.

Some diehards, such as streamer IShowSpeed , have actually travelled to New Zealand to play Grand Theft Auto 6 as soon as possible while others are toying with their console’s settings to bypass the geographical block.

Xbox users are going to their system settings and changing their location to New Zealand via the Language and Location menus before restarting their console.

Meanwhile PlayStation owners are having a trickier time taking a virtual visit to New Zealand. To play the game early, some users are creating a new PlayStation account based in New Zealand before buying a copy of GTA 6. They then need to enable ‘console sharing and offline play’ via their PlayStation’s ‘users and accounts’ sharing settings before they can play.

There were rumours circulating online that changing your location settings with either console might result in a ban, but social media has been flooded with success stories.

items.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
items.summary:
He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original

‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”

Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou

items.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
items.summary:
The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’

‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.”

On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers.”

items.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
items.summary:
Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary

Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that these physical media hold.

Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic. “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
items.summary:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote]

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

items.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
items.summary:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

Continue reading...
items.t: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this

items.title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
items.summary:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor.
